title: Pilgrimage: Bodh Gaya
hook: the Mahabodhi temple and the bodhi tree, full of pilgrims from every school

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first stop on pilgrimage: Lumbini, a garden and a king's stone pillar. Your line was where he was born. Which doorway became your gate? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

Before sunrise, the sound starts. A Tibetan monk sits on a cushion on the flagstones, reading aloud from a long, loose-leaf text. A few steps away, a group in white chants in Pali. Further on, Japanese pilgrims in a line strike a small hand drum. A woman from Thailand presses gold leaf onto a railing. Above them all rises a tall carved tower, and behind it, a broad tree with heart-shaped leaves, its branches propped up and draped in cloth. They do not all practice alike. They have all walked to the same tree. This is Bodh Gaya, the second stop on our pilgrimage, and the place they remember in plain words: here he woke up.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, MANY SCHOOLS.` → `A TOWER AND A TREE.` → `HERE HE WOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Start with why he went there. In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha looks back on his search. He had studied with teachers and left them, still unsatisfied. Then he walked until he reached Uruvela, and found what he calls a delightful grove, with a clear river and a village nearby for alms. A good place, he says, for someone set on striving. So he sat down. Note how plain that is. He did not pick a holy place. He picked a good place, and it became holy because of what happened there. Next, the tree. Bodhi means awakening. The tree is named for the night, not the other way around. In the opening of the monastic rule, the story picks up just after: the Buddha sitting at the foot of the bodhi tree by the river, newly awakened, staying on in the joy of freedom. The tree growing at Bodh Gaya today is not the same trunk. Tradition says it comes down from the first tree through cuttings carried and replanted, and pilgrims treat it with that care. Then the temple. The Mahabodhi temple rises beside the tree, and near it is a stone seat that marks where tradition says he sat. And here is the part a visitor carries home. At Bodh Gaya, Theravada, Tibetan, Zen, Pure Land and newer communities have built monasteries and practice side by side. On this path we have met the schools one at a time, chant by chant. At the tree, they share one shade.
screen: `A DELIGHTFUL GROVE BY A RIVER.` · `BODHI MEANS AWAKENING.` · `ONE TREE, MANY SCHOOLS.` · then, large: `HERE HE WOKE.`

segments.voice: This is the end of a week that took us from the hard days of a retreat, through metta and going home, through sesshin, and out to the garden at Lumbini. Here is a way to rest in all of it, if you'd like. Sit, and let your back be straight and easy. Picture the tree: wide branches, leaves trembling, the sound of many chants at once. Sit beneath it in your mind. You do not need to wake up today. Just sit where someone once did, and breathe. When your thoughts wander, come back to the leaves. The bell holds the time.
Pilgrimage. A journey to remember. Its second great stop is Bodh Gaya, where the tree and the temple mark the Buddha's awakening. Today's word.
Your line: where he woke. Today, find one ordinary good place, a bench, a step, a chair by a window, and sit there for one quiet minute. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Pilgrims from many Buddhist schools come to Bodh Gaya in India to circle the Mahabodhi temple, sit or prostrate near the bodhi tree, chant, and offer flowers, lamps and robes.

in his own account he chose a delightful grove, a good place to strive. it became holy afterward.

the tree at Bodh Gaya is named after the place
bodhi means awakening. the tree is named for what happened under it.

fork.setup: you've left your teachers, still searching. you reach a quiet grove with a clear river and a village nearby. what do you do?
options: keep walking to find a famous holy place.
go back to your old teachers.
fork.reveal: he sat down. in his own words, it was simply a good place for someone set on striving.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit bodhi: awakening. the tree takes its name from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bodh Gaya is a holy tree people visit.
what it means: the place Buddhists of many schools remember as where the Buddha woke, chosen at first simply as a good place to sit.
what a scholar hears: Uruvela in the Middle Length Discourses, the bodhi tree in the opening of the monastic rule, and a living tree tradition traces back to the first.

notes: MN 26 paraphrased: after leaving his teachers he reaches Uruvela (Senanigama) and finds a delightful grove with a clear river and a village for alms, 'suitable for striving'. Confirm.

Mahavagga 1.1 paraphrased: the Buddha at Uruvela on the bank of the Neranjara at the foot of the bodhi tree, just after awakening, experiencing the bliss of release. The number of days was cut per the claims rule. Confirm.
The present tree's descent from the original (via cuttings, traditionally through Sri Lanka) is attributed to tradition; confirm phrasing.
'A stone seat that marks where tradition says he sat' refers to the Vajrasana; confirm.
Hook scene (prostration boards, Pali chant, Japanese hand drums, Thai gold leaf) is illustrative; confirm it is fair to each school.
'On this path we have spent a whole year meeting the schools' refers to year four's theme; confirm acceptable under the claims rule.
Week end (days 1387–1393): the practice looks back over the week.
